rv.q: Sheehy’s originality makes an evocative play unmissable.
The other actors are uniformly superb in a play that is by turns, convulsively funny, bleak and puzzling.

A year after her Olivier-nominated performance in Machinal, Sheehy’s transformative, vanity and cliche-free turn here underscores how damn good she is and hopefully permanently elevates her to leading-actor status.
The leaps the takes as a writer into the numinous here won’t be to everyone’s taste but I bloody loved it.
I’m not sure it quite adds up, but it’s far more interesting than plenty of plays that do.
Still, somehow the plot of Air never takes a definitive shape.
There’s a joyous understatement in the colourful dabs of humour, tinged as they are with sadness and the profound regret for things either lost, or that never were.
It doesn’t quite make the impact McPherson might have hoped for then, but the play is still brimming with more fantasy and good fun than most.
It’s a frustrating play, always watchable, so nearly great, so nearly soaring, yet somehow held earthbound by the weight of its intent.
I can't say I was as moved by Air as I had hoped I might be, given McPherson's proven gift for the numinous.
That dog, like the play, is serviceable, but it’s not quite all you were hoping for.
It is a production that envelops you in the warmth and melancholy of rural Ireland, delivering a family drama that is as evocative as it is quietly magical.
Skipping over his adaptations, surely Air redeems that bald self-proscription.

With Rae Smith’s ghostly yet grounded design, helped by Mark Henderson’s lighting and Gregory Clarke’s sound, which create a real feel of the uncanny, Air is both elegiacally written and poetically resonant.

Unfortunately, there's hardly anything visually or narratively engaging about Air, other than for Gregory Clarke's sound design and Ben McQuinn on associate music capturing a beautiful, gentle and fascinating ambience which is never really replicated in McPherson's writing and direction, making for a tiring slog of a show instead.
Air fizzles at times with its own potential, but never truly bubbles over in this relaxed, sometimes-unfocused production.
The trouble is if the theme is inertia it needs a lot else to keep it interesting and I could never quite get my head round what Air was actually trying to be.

cn.t: McPherson's Chekhov-inspired Irish family drama divides critics, with some praising its mystical atmosphere and strong ensemble while others find it mellow and mundane—a slow-burn that doesn't always catch fire.
